title: Christian beginnings: Acts and the early witnesses
summary: The account in Acts provides the Christian beginnings to which later Anabaptist communities looked for their understanding of discipleship, baptism, and shared life.
paragraphs: The New Testament account of the first Christian communities stands at the beginning of this timeline. Its descriptions of baptism, fellowship, care for neighbours, and witness helped shape later Anabaptist readings of the church.

Martyrs’ Mirror reaches back to the early church to tell a story of faithful witness. These early Christians were not members of the sixteenth-century Anabaptist movement. The book’s claims about continuity belong to its historical and theological interpretation and should be read as such.

title: The Zürich baptisms

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: On 21 January 1525, Conrad Grebel baptized George Blaurock at a gathering associated with Felix Manz in Zürich. This is a central starting point for Swiss Anabaptist history.
paragraphs: A circle of reform-minded Christians in Zürich came to believe that baptism should follow a person’s own confession of faith. Their disagreement with the city’s religious settlement brought pressure to conform.

On 21 January 1525, Conrad Grebel baptized George Blaurock, and others at the gathering were then baptized. The event became a defining beginning for the Swiss Brethren. Anabaptism also developed in other regions, so the wider story includes several centres and traditions.

references.label: Mennonite World Conference: the first baptisms

title: Felix Manz and the cost of conviction

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: Felix Manz was drowned in Zürich on 5 January 1527. His story is central to the memory of persecution among the Swiss Brethren.
paragraphs: Felix Manz was one of the early Zürich advocates of believers’ baptism. He was executed by drowning in the Limmat on 5 January 1527.

The supplied Martyrs’ Mirror heading gives 1526 for Felix Mantz. That heading is preserved on the source page; this overview uses the date given in the later reference. Keeping both visible allows readers to examine the difference.

references.label: MWC: Testing Faith and Tradition (European history)

title: The Schleitheim Articles

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: The Schleitheim Articles set out seven points of agreement for a gathered Anabaptist community, including baptism, communion, church discipline, and refusal of the sword.
paragraphs: The 1527 Schleitheim Articles were written as a document of union. They are associated with Michael Sattler and the Swiss Brethren.

The articles address baptism, the ban, breaking of bread, separation, shepherds, the sword, and oaths. They help readers understand a form of Anabaptist discipleship while leaving room to investigate differences among other early groups.

paragraphs: Martyrs’ Mirror brings together a large collection of accounts spanning Christian beginnings and the persecution of Anabaptists. It preserves letters and testimonies as well as narrative accounts.

The book is a historical source with its own theological purpose. This archive preserves the supplied text, makes its sections searchable, and connects each section to the intact edition rather than silently rewriting its language or dates.

paragraphs: In August 1708, five men and three women gathered for baptism at the Eder River in Schwarzenau. Their movement combined influences from Anabaptism and Pietism.
This related history belongs in the wider timeline without treating every Brethren body as identical to the Mennonite, Amish, or Hutterite traditions.

title: Anabaptist history is still being written
summary: The present-day story includes communities across continents and many different traditions. Local histories, migrations, mission, and relationships between churches are part of the record still being gathered.
paragraphs: This site is an open historical archive for the wider Anabaptist family. It does not assume that one branch represents every community or that all relationships can be drawn as a simple line.

Modern history grows through documented contributions. Congregational records, dated testimonies, archive materials, and clearly credited photographs can help explain the people and events beyond the supplied timeline.

paragraphs: The Swiss Brethren emerged in the context of the Zürich baptisms and early Swiss Anabaptism. Later Swiss Mennonite and Amish histories share this background.

The later history includes refuge outside Switzerland and migration to other parts of Europe and North America. The branch explorer follows Swiss and South German ancestry into Mennonite and Amish histories, while the source accounts retain the names and experiences of individual witnesses.

title: Mennonite traditions

date.label: 1530s; a wider family name
date.basis: Period of Menno Simons’s leadership; the family name is not a single founding event.

summary: Mennonite history includes Dutch, Swiss, German, and later worldwide communities. Shared roots coexist with differences in worship, practice, organization, and relationships.
paragraphs: Mennonite history includes Dutch, Swiss, German, and later worldwide communities. Shared roots coexist with differences in worship, practice, organization, and relationships.

The name later came to describe a wider family that included Swiss and South German congregations as well as Dutch histories. The photographed chart distinguishes these migration lines and their subsequent conferences. No present-day denomination represents the entire Mennonite family.

references.label: Mennonite Church USA: history and traditions

title: Hutterite traditions

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: Hutterite history centres on gathered Christian communities and community of goods. Its migration story links Moravia, eastern Europe, and North America.
paragraphs: Hutterite history centres on gathered Christian communities and community of goods. Its migration story links Moravia, eastern Europe, and North America.

The exhibit follows Hutterite migrations across central and eastern Europe and into North America in 1874. Community of goods remains central to colony life. The later Bruderhof has a documented connection with Hutterite communal practice, but its own beginning was in Germany in 1920.

title: Amish traditions

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: Amish history grows from the Swiss Anabaptist tradition and the disagreements associated with Jakob Ammann. The later story includes migrations and distinct fellowships.
paragraphs: Amish history grows from the Swiss Anabaptist tradition and the disagreements associated with Jakob Ammann. The later story includes migrations and distinct fellowships.

The source chart follows later distinctions among Old Order Amish, Egly Amish, Beachy fellowships, and Amish Mennonite conferences. These names reflect disagreements and developments at different times; the 1693 division is the beginning of the wider Amish history, not the founding date of every later affiliation.

references.label: Mennonite Church USA: history and traditions

title: Schwarzenau Brethren

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: The Schwarzenau Brethren represent a related movement shaped by Anabaptism and Pietism, beginning with the baptisms at the Eder River in 1708.
paragraphs: The Schwarzenau Brethren represent a related movement shaped by Anabaptism and Pietism, beginning with the baptisms at the Eder River in 1708.

Alexander Mack was influenced by both Pietism and Anabaptism. Eight believers gathered for baptism in August 1708. Migration to Pennsylvania began in 1719, and a congregation formed at Germantown in 1723. Later divisions produced several Brethren bodies; the Church of the Brethren adopted that name in 1908.

title: Mennonite Brethren

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: The Mennonite Brethren arose through renewal among Mennonites in the Russian Empire. The tradition later developed across national boundaries.
paragraphs: The Mennonite Brethren arose through renewal among Mennonites in the Russian Empire. The tradition later developed across national boundaries.

The institutional history describes renewal and home Bible-study groups in the Molotschna settlement. In 1860 a distinct church organization emerged. Later migrations and mission activity carried the tradition beyond the Russian Empire. The exhibit’s other Brethren names belong to separate histories and are linked separately in the explorer.

title: Bruderhof

date.basis: Date of the event or documented activity; see cited sources

summary: The Bruderhof began in Germany in 1920. Its communal history later connected with the Hutterite tradition and developed its own community story.
paragraphs: The Bruderhof began in Germany in 1920. Its communal history later connected with the Hutterite tradition and developed its own community story.

Eberhard and Emmy Arnold and Else von Hollander began the community at Sannerz. Its subsequent story includes persecution in Germany and relocation across national boundaries. Its institutional history records both periods of fellowship with Hutterites and its later independent community life. The connection appears as a historical association rather than a direct sixteenth-century founding.

title: Waterlander Mennonites

date.label: Mid-sixteenth century; confession 1577
date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: A Dutch Mennonite stream associated with Waterland, with a confession of faith in 1577 and a distinctive approach to church discipline.
paragraphs: The Waterlanders developed within the Dutch Anabaptist movement in the middle of the sixteenth century. Their name refers to Waterland, north of Amsterdam. Differences over the severity of the ban and shunning distinguished them from other Dutch Mennonite groups.

Their 1577 confession sought agreement within the community and understanding with other Mennonites. It addresses faith and practical Christian living. The photographed timeline places Waterlanders beside Flemish and Frisian streams; these names describe changing historical fellowships, whose later relationships included attempts at reunion.

references.label: Waterlander Confession of Faith (1577), text and introduction

title: Flemish Mennonites

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: Flemish Mennonite communities formed one of the Dutch branches during sixteenth-century disagreements over discipline and congregational life.
paragraphs: Flemish and Frisian Mennonites divided at Franeker in 1566. The name Flemish reflected the background of believers who had moved from the southern Netherlands. Disagreements were about community practice as well as regional identity.

The Flemish stream itself developed different fellowships. Reunion efforts brought Old and Mild Flemish together in 1632, followed by union with the Frisian–High German group in 1639. The source chart also follows Dutch communities east into the Vistula region. A branch name on the chart therefore represents a history of both division and renewed fellowship.

title: Frisian Mennonites

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: A Dutch Mennonite branch that developed in Friesland and also took root in West Prussia.
paragraphs: The Frisian–Flemish division began at Franeker in 1566, following disagreements between local Mennonites and believers who had arrived from the southern Netherlands. The Frisian name became a fellowship designation as well as a geographical description.

Frisian communities were themselves diverse. Some maintained especially strict church discipline, while others participated in wider union efforts. Their history continued in the Netherlands and West Prussia. The photographed chart traces these lines alongside the Flemish and Waterlander branches rather than presenting Dutch Anabaptism as a single uniform body.

title: Russian Mennonite communities

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: Communities established in the Russian Empire developed several church traditions and later migrated to the Americas and elsewhere.
paragraphs: Prussian Mennonite settlers established Chortitza near the end of the eighteenth century. The archives preserve letters between the early settlers and the communities they had left, including correspondence dated 1789. Later settlements included Molotschna. Much of this history took place in what is now Ukraine; Russian Mennonite is a historical cultural description, not a claim that every community was ethnically Russian.

The exhibit follows several different lines from these settlements: congregational Mennonites, Mennonite Brethren, Kleine Gemeinde, and Old Colony communities. Migration, war, and political repression carried their histories beyond the Russian Empire. These branches retained different practices and developed new fellowships in their later homes.

references.label: Mennonite Heritage Archives: early Chortitza correspondence

title: Old Colony Mennonites

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: Old Colony history connects the Chortitza settlement with later migrations and a wider family of colony-based Mennonite churches.
paragraphs: Old Colony refers historically to Chortitza, the older Mennonite settlement in the Russian Empire. The photographed exhibit also uses Old Colony Groups as a broad heading for several related conservative communities. That heading should not erase the differences between Old Colony, Bergthal, Chortitzer, Sommerfeld, and other churches.

The chart follows migration to Canada in the 1870s and later moves to Latin America. Families sought places where their faith, schools, language, and communal arrangements could continue. The branch explorer provides separate entries for the named Bergthal, Chortitzer, and Sommerfeld lines, allowing readers to follow these relationships without treating them as interchangeable.

references.label: Mennonite Heritage Archives: Chortitza settlement documents

title: Old Order Mennonites

date.label: Regional divisions 1872–1901
date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: Old Order Mennonite fellowships developed through several regional divisions beginning in the later nineteenth century.
paragraphs: In 1872, Jacob Wisler and supporters organized separate conferences in Indiana and Ohio after conflict over innovations in Mennonite church life. Related divisions followed in Ontario in 1889, Pennsylvania in 1893, and Virginia in 1901.

Old Order is a family description, not one worldwide conference. Congregations emphasize ordered community life and retain differing rules concerning dress, transportation, and technology. The source chart names several later groups on this line. The Ontario archive’s records provide an entry into the regional story without assuming that every Old Order fellowship follows identical practices.

references.label: Mennonite Archives of Ontario: Old Order administrative history

title: General Conference Mennonite Church

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: A Mennonite conference shown on the exhibit’s North American timeline; its U.S. congregations joined in forming Mennonite Church USA in 2002.
paragraphs: The General Conference Mennonite Church developed a cooperative conference history alongside the older Mennonite Church. The exhibit dates its organization to 1860 and follows its educational, mission, and congregational life.

The two bodies retained distinct histories before their U.S. congregations formed Mennonite Church USA in 2002. The archive preserves the historical General Conference name so readers can understand the source chart. Institutional records provide further detail on the congregations and agencies involved.

title: Church of God in Christ, Mennonite

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: John Holdeman and others began worshiping separately in Ohio in 1859, forming a distinct Mennonite church history.
paragraphs: John Holdeman of Wayne County, Ohio, urged spiritual renewal in the Mennonite church. In 1859 he and others began worshiping separately; the community developed as the Church of God in Christ, Mennonite. Holdeman traveled as an evangelist and wrote Mirror of Truth.

The church’s own account emphasizes believers’ baptism, nonresistance, conversion, modest life, and congregational discipline. Later congregations and missions extended beyond North America. Its account of continuity with earlier Christians expresses the church’s theological understanding; the explorer dates the documented organizational beginning to 1859.

references.label: Church of God in Christ, Mennonite: its own history

title: Conservative Amish Mennonites: Rosedale Network

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: Ministers meeting at Pigeon, Michigan, formed the Conservative Amish Mennonite Conference in 1910; its history continues as Rosedale Network.
paragraphs: Ministers from Pigeon, Michigan, Belleville, Pennsylvania, and Hartville, Ohio, gathered in 1910 to support unity among Amish Mennonite congregations. They valued local congregational authority while seeking ways to work together.

The conference developed education, mission, and service work. Its historical name appears on the exhibit, while its present institutional history is published as Rosedale Network of Churches. This conference is one Amish Mennonite development; it does not encompass every fellowship described as conservative Mennonite.

title: Beachy Amish fellowships

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: The Beachy Amish history began with a 1927 division in an Amish congregation in Somerset County, Pennsylvania.
paragraphs: Moses M. Beachy’s congregation in Somerset County, Pennsylvania, became the setting of a division in 1927. The disagreement concerned church discipline, including the treatment of members who moved to other Anabaptist congregations.

The Beachy name later described a wider fellowship of Amish Mennonite congregations. Their later practices and mission activity should not be read back into every detail of the original dispute. The exhibit places Beachy on the Amish line; the historical account by Alvin J. Beachy offers a closer view of the local beginnings.

references.label: Alvin J. Beachy: The Rise and Development of the Beachy Amish Mennonite Churches (1955)

title: Old Order Amish

date.label: Later nineteenth century
date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: Old Order Amish identity developed during nineteenth-century disagreements over conference organization and changes in church life.
paragraphs: The Amish tradition began with the late-seventeenth-century division associated with Jakob Ammann. Old Order Amish is a later designation that became prominent during nineteenth-century differences over proposed changes and ministerial conference cooperation.

The exhibit places Old Order Amish alongside Egly Amish, Amish Mennonite conferences, and later Beachy fellowships. These separate lines help explain why Amish is a family of histories rather than one organizational body. Local congregations establish their own rules, and particular practices differ among affiliations.

references.label: Rosedale Network: the Amish Mennonite conference background

title: Conservative Mennonite fellowships

date.label: Twentieth-century family; multiple beginnings
date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: A broad family of Mennonite fellowships maintaining distinctive church practices, with several different conference histories.
paragraphs: Conservative Mennonite describes several fellowships rather than one denomination with a single founding date. The photographed chart shows older Mennonite and Amish Mennonite lines from which different conservative histories developed.

These communities place importance on believers’ baptism, nonresistance, church discipline, and daily Christian practice. Dress, worship, organization, and relationships with other congregations vary. The Rosedale conference has its own dated history and should not be used as the name or origin of every conservative Mennonite group. This overview therefore uses a broad twentieth-century period, with particular fellowships identified separately in the explorer.

references.label: Mennonite Church USA: FAQ on different Mennonite traditions

title: Dutch Mennonite Conference: ADS

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: The Algemene Doopsgezinde Sociëteit brought Dutch Mennonite congregations into a shared association in 1811.
paragraphs: The Algemene Doopsgezinde Sociëteit (ADS) was founded in 1811 to support the training of ministers and provide financial help to congregations in need. The exhibit calls this continuing Dutch association the Dutch Mennonite Conference.

Its history belongs to the later cooperation of Dutch Mennonite congregations whose earlier names included Waterlander, Flemish, and Frisian. The association’s own account explains its shared structures and purposes. The explorer treats this as cooperation across older streams, with the individual congregations and historical distinctions still visible.

title: Evangelical Mennonite Brethren

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: A fellowship organized in North America in 1889, later named the Fellowship of Evangelical Bible Churches.
paragraphs: Aaron Wall of Mountain Lake, Minnesota, and Isaac Peters of Henderson, Nebraska, provided leadership to congregations shaped by renewal among Mennonites from the Russian Empire. Their first convention met on 14 October 1889. Three congregations joined in the new fellowship.

The fellowship emphasized conversion, biblical authority, church discipline, and evangelism. Its name became Fellowship of Evangelical Bible Churches in 1987. The institutional history and historical sketches record its development. The explorer keeps this line separate from both the Mennonite Brethren movement founded in 1860 and the Canadian conferences with similar evangelical names.

references.label: Evangelical Mennonite Brethren: archival authority record

title: Evangelical Mennonite Conference

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: The Canadian Kleine Gemeinde adopted the name Evangelical Mennonite Conference in 1960.
paragraphs: The Canadian conference traces its roots to the Kleine Gemeinde movement of 1812 and the migration to Manitoba in 1874–1875. It adopted the name Evangelical Mennonite Church in 1952 and Evangelical Mennonite Conference in 1960.

Its archival collection documents conferences, missions, publications, and congregational life. These names belong to this Canadian history; the similarly named Evangelical Mennonite Mission Conference and Evangelical Mennonite Brethren have different beginnings and appear separately in the explorer.

references.label: EMC: Circling the Globe, conference history

title: Rudnerweider Mennonites

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: A renewal movement among Sommerfeld Mennonites organized as the Rudnerweider church in 1937.
paragraphs: The Rudnerweider church emerged from a division in the Sommerfeld church over the desire for renewal. Its official archival description dates organization to 1937. The photographed chart marks the preceding movement in 1936, distinguishing the beginning of renewal from formal organization.

The church became the Evangelical Mennonite Mission Conference in 1959. Its records preserve conference activity, congregational life, missions, and research for the history Search for Renewal. The explorer shows the new conference name as a continuation of this particular fellowship.

title: Charity Ministries and related fellowships

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: Charity Christian Fellowship began in Lancaster County in 1982 and developed a sermon ministry reaching wider fellowships.
paragraphs: Charity Christian Fellowship’s own account dates its beginning to 1982, when Mose Stoltzfus and Denny Kenaston established the congregation. It describes a desire for revived New Testament church life, followed by sermon distribution and mission work.

The sermon ministry developed from cassette distribution, took the name Charity Gospel Tape Ministry in 1990, and later became Charity Ministries. It became a joint ministry with Ephrata Christian Fellowship in 2001. Reorganization was proposed at the end of 2010, and the two churches began operating their own sermon ministries in November 2011.

The site owner identifies this wider fellowship history as part of the background to the community supporting this archive. The local Agape account is recorded separately; the published sermon-ministry reorganization does not by itself establish the details of that local division.

references.label: Charity Christian Fellowship: its own history

title: Agape fellowships

date.label: c. 2010 (owner’s account)
date.basis: Approximate date and relationship supplied by the site owner; additional institutional details are not inferred.

summary: The supporting fellowship’s own account places the Agape stream within its Charity-related background around 2010.
paragraphs: The site owner describes a division around 2010 in the Charity-related fellowships, with the Agape stream forming part of the background to this site. This is an attributed community account. The approximate date identifies the period described rather than an independently verified incorporation or founding date.

Charity Christian Fellowship’s published history separately documents a sermon-ministry reorganization proposed in 2010 and implemented in November 2011 with Ephrata Christian Fellowship. That published event provides contemporary context, but it should not be substituted for the owner’s account of the Agape relationship.
The explorer includes this local account alongside the wider Anabaptist family. Additional congregational records and firsthand accounts can extend it through the page’s contribution link.

title: Danzig and Prussian Mennonites

date.label: Sixteenth-century settlement
date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: Mennonite communities in the Vistula region linked Dutch Anabaptist histories with later migrations into the Russian Empire.
paragraphs: The photographed timeline follows Dutch Mennonite lines into Danzig and Prussia. Congregations in the Vistula region included differing Flemish and Frisian traditions, so this geographical label does not identify a single denomination.

Letters preserved by Mennonite Heritage Archives connect Prussian congregations with the early Chortitza settlement. They include correspondence from 1789 and a 1791 letter from the Danzig Flemish church. These documents let readers follow migration through the voices of the communities involved. The chart also records the disruption of Danzig and Prussian congregations during the Second World War and continuing congregations in northwestern Germany.

references.label: Mennonite Heritage Archives: early Chortitza correspondence

title: Bergthal Mennonites

date.label: Colony established 1836; registers from 1843
date.basis: Colony beginning shown on the photographed timeline; surviving registers dated by the cited archive.

summary: The Bergthal colony’s migration to Manitoba became the background of the Chortitzer and Sommerfeld church histories.
paragraphs: The exhibit places Bergthal within the colony-based Mennonite family of the Russian Empire. Surviving Bergthal church registers begin in 1843, providing a record of families and community membership.

Almost the entire colony moved to Manitoba in 1874–1876. Its East Reserve church became known as Chortitzer. Migration across the Red River to the West Reserve and later disagreements produced further church relationships. Bergthal therefore describes a historical community whose members contributed to several later fellowships, rather than one unchanging organizational line.

title: Chortitzer Mennonites

date.label: Manitoba settlement 1874–1876
date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: The Bergthal migration to Manitoba’s East Reserve in 1874–1876 established the Chortitzer church history.
paragraphs: Chortitzer congregational history in Manitoba grew from the arrival of Bergthal Mennonites in 1874–1876. The Mennonite Heritage Archives holds church registers, correspondence, financial records, and materials concerning the Waisenamt, the community’s estate and guardianship administration.

Further migrations and changing relationships with West Reserve congregations form part of this history. In 1926–1927, members of the Chortitzer and Sommerfeld churches helped establish the Menno colony in Paraguay. The source chart shows these movements within the wider colony-based family. The name also belongs to a continuing church history later known as Christian Mennonite Conference.

title: Sommerfeld Mennonites

date.label: 1890s
date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: A West Reserve Mennonite church associated with Bergthal migration and later colony and renewal movements.
paragraphs: Bergthal families settling on Manitoba’s West Reserve were connected with the East Reserve church. Disagreement in the West Reserve led to distinct church organizations, including the Sommerfeld church, shown on the photographed timeline in the 1890s.

Its story includes migration to Latin America and the renewal movement that became the Rudnerweider church. The archives distinguish Sommerfeld from Chortitzer, Bergthal, and Old Colony organizations. These names identify related but separate community histories; the explorer follows those particular connections.

references.label: Sommerfeld Mennonite Church of Manitoba: archival history

title: Kleine Gemeinde

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: A reform movement in the Molotschna settlement that began in 1812 under Klaas Reimer and later developed different national histories.
paragraphs: Klaas Reimer and other Mennonites in Molotschna organized the Kleine Gemeinde, or Little Church, in 1812. They sought reform in church discipline and Christian life. Families migrated to Canada in 1874–1875.

The Canadian history later led to the Evangelical Mennonite Conference. Other communities retained the Kleine Gemeinde name, including congregations in Mexico. The shared beginning should therefore be read alongside the different later developments, rather than identifying all Kleine Gemeinde congregations with one present-day conference.

references.label: Evangelical Mennonite Conference fonds: administrative history

title: Evangelical Mennonite Mission Conference

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: The Rudnerweider church adopted the Evangelical Mennonite Mission Conference identity on 1 July 1959.
paragraphs: The conference continues the Rudnerweider movement organized in 1937. Its archival description dates the Evangelical Mennonite Mission Conference to 1 July 1959.

The official repository preserves materials from the Rudnerweider period and the later conference, including mission work and congregational records. The chart places this line among the colony-based Mennonite histories. Its similar name should be distinguished from the Evangelical Mennonite Conference, which grew from Kleine Gemeinde.

title: Mennonite Church: MC

date.label: North American development, eighteenth century
date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: The older Mennonite Church in North America developed from Swiss and German congregational histories.
paragraphs: The exhibit distinguishes Mennonite Church (MC) from General Conference Mennonite Church (GC). The older MC history belongs especially to Swiss and German congregations in North America, with migrations and settlement during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.

The label describes a historical church body, rather than every church called Mennonite. In 2002, its U.S. congregations and those of the General Conference formed Mennonite Church USA. Other fellowships and national histories continued along their own paths.

title: Mennonite Church USA

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: Mennonite Church USA formed in 2002 through the union of U.S. congregations of MC and GC.
paragraphs: Mennonite Church USA was formed in 2002 when U.S. congregations from the Mennonite Church and General Conference Mennonite Church joined in a new denomination.

Its historical archives preserve both predecessor histories. This union supplies one present-day destination for the two older lines on the exhibit. The broader Anabaptist family includes many other conferences and independent fellowships, so this node represents one union rather than a universal endpoint.

title: Reformed Mennonites

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: A distinct North American Mennonite fellowship led by John Herr from 1812.
paragraphs: The photographed chart marks the Reformed Mennonite Church as a separate line beginning in 1812. John Herr’s followers sought stricter fidelity to their understanding of the church and Christian discipline.

Reformed Mennonite is a particular historical name. It should be distinguished from the later Old Order conferences and from Reformed Protestant churches. The chart follows this community beside the older Mennonite Church, providing a starting point for exploring its distinctive history.

references.label: Historical reference: Mennonites, New International Encyclopaedia

title: Mennonites of Swiss–South German ancestry

date.label: Migration history, seventeenth–eighteenth centuries
date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: Migrations connected Swiss and South German Anabaptist communities with European refuges and later congregations in North America.
paragraphs: The photographed timeline follows Swiss and South German Anabaptist communities through persecution, refuge, and migration. The shared ancestry label describes several congregational histories, including later Mennonite and Amish developments.

Swiss and German Mennonites migrated to Pennsylvania during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries and later settled farther west. Language, family networks, and congregational traditions traveled with them. This geographical history is kept distinct from the Dutch–Prussian–Russian migration line, while later cooperation between their churches remains visible.

title: Brethren in Christ: River Brethren

date.label: Beginnings 1775–1788
date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: A Pennsylvania movement with Anabaptist and Pietist roots that emerged between 1775 and 1788.
paragraphs: The Brethren in Christ began near Marietta in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, between 1775 and 1788. Their Anabaptist background interacted with Pietist emphases on personal faith and transformed life. Neighbors called them River Brethren because many lived along the Susquehanna River.

Later history included migration, mission, and engagement with Wesleyan Holiness and evangelical movements. The chart places this related stream alongside Mennonite histories. It is distinct from the Schwarzenau Brethren, whose beginning was in Germany in 1708, and from the Mennonite Brethren of the Russian Empire.

references.label: Brethren in Christ Historical Society: history

title: Egly Amish and Evangelical Mennonite Church

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: Henry Egly’s Amish reform movement developed into the Defenseless Mennonites and later the Evangelical Mennonite Church.
paragraphs: Henry Egly led a group from an Amish congregation in Indiana in 1866, emphasizing new birth and salvation by faith. The movement became known as Egly Amish and adopted the Defenseless Mennonite name in 1908.

Its later name was Evangelical Mennonite Church, followed by Fellowship of Evangelical Churches in 2003. The institutional history describes education, service, and mission developments. The explorer preserves the older exhibit name and its Amish background, distinguishing it from the Canadian Evangelical Mennonite Conference.

references.label: Fellowship of Evangelical Churches: institutional history

title: United Missionary Church and Missionary Church

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: The exhibit’s Mennonite Brethren in Christ line developed into United Missionary Church and joined a union in 1969.
paragraphs: The photographed chart follows nineteenth-century evangelical and holiness renewal through the Mennonite Brethren in Christ name. The Missionary Church’s own chronology records earlier unions of Mennonite-related groups and later adoption of the United Missionary Church name.

In 1969 the United Missionary Church united with the Missionary Church Association to form the Missionary Church. The explorer marks this as a union of particular organizations and a related history influenced by several traditions. It should be distinguished from Brethren in Christ and Mennonite Brethren, despite the resemblance of the older names.

title: Soviet Mennonites: Kirchliche and Brethren

date.label: Soviet period 1917–1991
date.basis: Historical period represented by the exhibit; not a church founding date.

summary: The chart follows Mennonite and Mennonite Brethren communities through revolution, war, repression, and migration in the Soviet period.
paragraphs: The exhibit uses USSR “Kirchliche” and Mennonite Brethren for communities continuing in the Soviet Union. Kirchliche distinguished congregational Mennonites from the Brethren movement; the label is not a new denomination founded in 1917.

The timeline records the Russian Revolution, migrations during the 1920s, wartime displacement, and continuing believers under Soviet rule. This page covers the historical period 1917–1991. Family and church records need to be read within those changing political conditions, with the different congregational traditions kept visible.

title: Mennonite Central Committee

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: Mennonite Central Committee began in 1920 as a cooperative response to hunger among communities in Ukraine.
paragraphs: North American church leaders met in July 1920 to coordinate help for hungry people in Ukraine. The committee’s first official meeting followed on 27 September 1920.

The source chart includes MCC beside Mennonite World Conference because cooperation and service also belong to the family’s history. MCC is a relief and service organization, rather than a denomination or a branch produced by church division. Its archival record follows the development of this shared work.

references.label: Centre for Mennonite Brethren Studies: MCC records

title: Mennonite World Conference

date.basis: Dated beginning or period described by the cited source; a period is not an exact founding date.

summary: A global fellowship established in 1925 to connect Anabaptist churches across national and tradition boundaries.
paragraphs: The exhibit marks Mennonite World Conference beginning in 1925 and follows later assemblies. This line represents shared fellowship among churches, rather than a denomination replacing the older traditions.

Its work connects churches within the wider Anabaptist family. The explorer includes it as a cooperative institution alongside the different streams, and the timeline’s global map points beyond European and North American migrations to churches on other continents.

title: Mennonite migration to Germantown

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: The 1683 Germantown settlement opened an important North American chapter in Mennonite migration.
paragraphs: The photographed timeline marks Mennonite settlement at Germantown, Pennsylvania, in 1683. Later migrations from Swiss and German communities brought further congregations to Pennsylvania and beyond. Different migration waves are shown separately from the Dutch–Prussian–Russian history.

title: Settlement at Chortitza

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: Communities established in the Russian Empire developed several church traditions and later migrated to the Americas and elsewhere.
paragraphs: Prussian Mennonite settlers established Chortitza near the end of the eighteenth century. The archives preserve letters between the early settlers and the communities they had left, including correspondence dated 1789. Later settlements included Molotschna. Much of this history took place in what is now Ukraine; Russian Mennonite is a historical cultural description, not a claim that every community was ethnically Russian.

title: John Holdeman’s separate fellowship

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: John Holdeman and others began worshiping separately in Ohio in 1859, forming a distinct Mennonite church history.
paragraphs: John Holdeman of Wayne County, Ohio, urged spiritual renewal in the Mennonite church. In 1859 he and others began worshiping separately; the community developed as the Church of God in Christ, Mennonite. Holdeman traveled as an evangelist and wrote Mirror of Truth.

title: Old Order Mennonite regional divisions

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: Old Order Mennonite fellowships developed through several regional divisions beginning in the later nineteenth century.
paragraphs: In 1872, Jacob Wisler and supporters organized separate conferences in Indiana and Ohio after conflict over innovations in Mennonite church life. Related divisions followed in Ontario in 1889, Pennsylvania in 1893, and Virginia in 1901.

title: The Beachy Amish division

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: The Beachy Amish history began with a 1927 division in an Amish congregation in Somerset County, Pennsylvania.
paragraphs: Moses M. Beachy’s congregation in Somerset County, Pennsylvania, became the setting of a division in 1927. The disagreement concerned church discipline, including the treatment of members who moved to other Anabaptist congregations.

title: Rudnerweider church organization

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: A renewal movement among Sommerfeld Mennonites organized as the Rudnerweider church in 1937.
paragraphs: The Rudnerweider church emerged from a division in the Sommerfeld church over the desire for renewal. Its official archival description dates organization to 1937. The photographed chart marks the preceding movement in 1936, distinguishing the beginning of renewal from formal organization.

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: The Rudnerweider church adopted the Evangelical Mennonite Mission Conference identity on 1 July 1959.
paragraphs: The conference continues the Rudnerweider movement organized in 1937. Its archival description dates the Evangelical Mennonite Mission Conference to 1 July 1959.

title: Evangelical Mennonite Conference name

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: The Canadian Kleine Gemeinde adopted the name Evangelical Mennonite Conference in 1960.
paragraphs: The Canadian conference traces its roots to the Kleine Gemeinde movement of 1812 and the migration to Manitoba in 1874–1875. It adopted the name Evangelical Mennonite Church in 1952 and Evangelical Mennonite Conference in 1960.

title: Charity Christian Fellowship begins

date.basis: Milestone described by the cited institutional history or supplied timeline.

summary: Charity Christian Fellowship began in Lancaster County in 1982 and developed a sermon ministry reaching wider fellowships.
paragraphs: Charity Christian Fellowship’s own account dates its beginning to 1982, when Mose Stoltzfus and Denny Kenaston established the congregation. It describes a desire for revived New Testament church life, followed by sermon distribution and mission work.

title: The regional roots of Anabaptism

date.label: 1520s: several regional beginnings
date.basis: Regional beginnings summarized by the supplied timeline; no single institutional founder is implied.

summary: Anabaptism developed in several regions during the Radical Reformation, including Switzerland, South Germany and Austria, and the Netherlands.
paragraphs: The photographed timeline begins with several lines in the 1520s. The Zürich baptisms are a defining event for the Swiss Brethren; other Anabaptist communities formed in different political and religious settings. The common Anabaptist name should therefore be read as a family of regional beginnings.

The explorer uses this entry to group early regional streams. Its connecting lines indicate emergence within the Radical Reformation, rather than descent of every stream from one Zürich congregation. The earlier Christian and medieval accounts in Martyrs’ Mirror remain linked through the era timeline, where their historical setting and the book’s interpretation are visible.
